projects.title: RubHew
projects.tagline: Campus delivery marketplace — students carry canteen orders back for each other
projects.context: Final project, CS369 Web Application Development
projects.summary: I owned the backend end to end while leading the team. The design problem that shaped everything: two parties act on the same order at different times, so one status field was never going to be enough.

highlights.text: Designed and implemented the backend: an 18-endpoint API over route, controller and model layers, session authentication with bcrypt, and all database operations.
Modelled the two-sided order lifecycle as independent delivery and payment state machines advanced by different parties, with per-carrier capacity and fees applied at pricing time.
Reviewed and tested frontend features contributed by the rest of the team before merge.

engineering.architecture: Backend and Frontend are separate npm packages talking over CRA's dev proxy. The backend is ESM Express 5 in three layers — app.js registers routes, controllers.js holds all eighteen handlers, models.js owns the schemas and connection — over three collections: User, Order, Menu. The modelling choice worth explaining is that a 'carry my order' post is not its own collection: a post IS a User with availablefororder > 0, so the feed is a query over users.

decisions.what: Two independent state machines on one order rather than one combined status.
decisions.why: Delivery (buying → delivering → delivered) is advanced only by the carrier; payment (unpaid → pending → paid) is claimed by the buyer and confirmed by the carrier. Two parties, two transitions.
decisions.instead: A single enum encoding the cross product of both.

decisions.what: Server-side sessions over JWT, storing both username and studentId.
decisions.why: Handlers scope every query by student without a second lookup. Passwords are bcrypt at cost 10 — a deliberate correction of the unsalted SHA-256 I used in the earlier Library project.
decisions.instead: Stateless signed tokens.

decisions.what: Pricing happens after ordering, not before.
decisions.why: The buyer cannot know shop prices, so they submit items unpriced; the carrier fills unit prices at the counter and the total recomputes as base fee plus (unit price + per-item fee) × count.
decisions.instead: A fixed menu with prices set upfront.

decisions.what: Documents related by studentId string, with no ObjectId refs and no populate.
decisions.why: Every join stays an explicit second query, which keeps the data flow readable.
decisions.instead: Mongoose refs — at the cost of referential integrity Mongo will not enforce either way.

projects.title: Video Frame Stitching Tool
projects.tagline: Panorama stitcher built from primitives: SIFT/ORB features, RANSAC homographies, feathered blending
projects.summary: No cv2.Stitcher. Every stage is assembled from primitives so each can be swapped and compared — detector, matcher, ratio test, RANSAC, chaining, canvas, blend. The pipeline streams, holding two frames of features and one warped frame at a time, because a long pan otherwise takes the canvas and the RAM with it.

highlights.text: Built a panorama stitcher from the underlying operations rather than a library stitcher: SIFT and ORB backends behind one interface, Lowe's ratio test over kNN matches, and RANSAC homography estimation per frame pair.

Chained pairwise homographies into a global reference frame with middle-frame re-centering, rejecting implausible transforms via SVD conditioning and projected-corner geometry before they could corrupt the chain.
Implemented streaming warp and blend: a canvas auto-sized from projected frame corners, feathered alpha weighting, and a running weighted average that holds one frame at a time.
Wrapped it in a CLI that extracts frames with ffmpeg, runs all four detector-matcher combinations into separate folders for comparison, and re-encodes an annotated H.264 walkthrough.

engineering.architecture: Ten modules under stitch/, one per pipeline stage, wired by main.py. features.py exposes SIFT and ORB behind a Protocol that also carries a DescriptorSpec; matching.py reads that spec to pick metric and index; geometry.py estimates and chains homographies; warp.py sizes the canvas and blends. It streams by design: keypoints and descriptors are held for exactly two frames, and the blend accumulates into one float32 buffer pair rather than collecting warped frames.

decisions.what: Assembled from primitives rather than calling cv2.Stitcher.
decisions.why: Every stage stays separable, so all four detector×matcher combinations can run over the same frames into separate output folders and be compared directly.
decisions.instead: One library call that works and teaches nothing.

decisions.what: Descriptor type drives matcher configuration instead of being hardcoded.
decisions.why: SIFT is tagged FLOAT and ORB BINARY, so the matcher picks NORM_L2 vs NORM_HAMMING and KD-tree vs LSH. KD-tree FLANN on ORB is a real mistake — those trees assume Euclidean geometry, and binary descriptors are not in that space.
decisions.instead: A hardcoded matcher, which silently degrades on one of the two backends.

decisions.what: Consecutive-pair homographies chained, with the global reference at the middle frame rather than frame 0.
decisions.why: Neighbouring frames overlap heavily so their matches are reliable; re-centering on the middle splits accumulated drift across both halves instead of piling it at one end.
decisions.instead: Matching every frame to a single reference — fewer drift compounds, far weaker matches.

decisions.what: Feathering by Gaussian blur of the validity mask rather than a distance transform.
decisions.why: Full-canvas distanceTransform per frame was the bottleneck on wide panoramas; the separable blur gives the same soft edge far cheaper.
decisions.instead: distanceTransform — more correct, measurably too slow here.

projects.title: Three.js Shooter
projects.tagline: WebGL2 first-person shooter with rigid-body physics and continuous enemy spawning
projects.summary: The interesting part is the seam between two systems that each want to own an object's position: the physics world and the render scene graph. I built both sides and the gameplay layer on top of them.

highlights.text: Built the 3D renderer with Three.js on WebGL2 and integrated cannon-es for rigid-body physics, reconciling the render scene and the physics world every frame.
Implemented model importing, enemy spawning and steering, the projectile manager, and all core gameplay logic.

engineering.architecture: One ES module, no build step. Two worlds are maintained in parallel by hand — a THREE.Scene for rendering and a CANNON.World for simulation — with every entity a {body, mesh} pair held in one of two arrays, so the body's position can be copied onto its mesh each tick. The frame loop runs a fixed order: read buffered input, step the world at 1/60, attach the camera to the player body, update both entity arrays, render.

decisions.what: Two engines kept in manual sync rather than one.
decisions.why: Three.js renders and cannon-es simulates, with body.position copied onto mesh.position every frame.
decisions.instead: Bounding-box collision in Three.js alone — cheaper, but no solver, no restitution, no inter-entity contacts.

decisions.what: Enemies steered by writing a normalised direction-to-player vector into body.velocity, not by translating the mesh.
decisions.why: The solver then handles enemies pushing each other apart when they bunch up. This is steering, not pathfinding — the arena is open, so there is nothing to path around.
decisions.instead: Lerping mesh positions directly, which gives no inter-enemy collision at all.

decisions.what: Input buffered into a keys object and only acted on inside the frame loop.
decisions.why: Acting in the keydown handler couples movement speed to the OS key-repeat rate — that earlier version is still in the repo as backup.js.
decisions.instead: Direct handling in the event callback.

projects.title: Begin OpenGL
projects.tagline: C++ renderer built from scratch: GLSL shader pipeline, CMake build, textured geometry
projects.summary: No engine, no framework. The original work here is the shader abstraction — file loading, compile and link with per-stage status checks, typed uniform setters — written to understand the pipeline rather than consume it. The README is a dated diary of what defeated me along the way.

highlights.text: Wrote the shader abstraction by hand: file loading with stream exception masks, compile and link with per-stage status checks and info-log reporting, and typed uniform setters.
Set up a C++ build pipeline with CMake, linking GLFW, OpenGL and X11 dependencies.
Integrated stb_image texture loading and applied multi-unit texturing to 3D cube meshes, with frame-rate-independent camera movement via delta time.

engineering.architecture: Four source files, no abstraction layers. main.cpp holds main(), every GLFW callback and the texture loader, following the numbered plan commented at the top: window setup, vertex preparation, shader, texture, render loop. Shader is the one real class, wrapping compile/link and the typed uniform setters. State the GLFW callbacks need sits at file scope, because C callbacks cannot capture.

decisions.what: Raw OpenGL with dependencies vendored into include/ rather than fetched by the build.
decisions.why: The point was to see each stage of the pipeline, not to have a framework hide it.
decisions.instead: GLFW as a git submodule — the README's own todo records this as deferred, not overlooked.

decisions.what: Dynamic linking against a prebuilt lib/libglfw.so rather than static.
decisions.why: Diary, 17/10/2025: the statically linked binary would not run on another machine, so shipping it in the repo was pointless, and I had not learned dynamic linking properly yet.
decisions.instead: Static linking, which I tried first.

decisions.what: Shader source read from disk at runtime by relative path, so the binary only runs from the project root.
decisions.why: Diary, 28/10/2025: portable file reading in C++ defeated me and direct paths were the stopgap.
decisions.instead: Embedding the GLSL as string literals, or resolving paths relative to the executable.

decisions.what: The cube is 36 explicit vertices with no index buffer.
decisions.why: Started with an EBO and dropped it — main.h still carries the commented-out loadBuffer signature that took an index array.
decisions.instead: Indexed drawing, which is what I would use now.

projects.title: Library Web Application
projects.tagline: Relational schema and borrow/reserve/return service for a library system
projects.summary: My largest team at nine people. Most of the design effort went into the data model, built around the lifecycle a physical book moves through — available, borrowed, reserved, returned, awaiting staff confirmation — with the API as a thin layer over it.

highlights.text: Designed the entity-relationship model and derived the relational algebra behind library services such as book reservation.
Implemented the backend and API layer with Node.js and Express, covering the borrow, reserve, return and staff-confirmation lifecycle, quota accounting, search, and the review and rating system.
Split schema ownership across a nine-person team while keeping the model coherent, resolving conflicting table designs before they reached implementation.

engineering.architecture: Two layers, no more. server.js is a single 1,031-line Express file holding every route, every query, the connection, the session config and the view engine. Rendering is split two ways: /book and /profile are server-rendered EJS, while every other page is a static HTML file that fetches JSON and builds its DOM client-side. Eight MySQL tables, with role modelled as row-existence in a librarian table rather than a column.

decisions.what: Role as row-existence in a librarian table, re-queried on every protected route.
decisions.why: Keeps role assignment a data operation rather than a schema change, at the cost of one extra query per request.
decisions.instead: A role column on users, or a flag cached in the session — the hardcoded username check it replaced is still there commented out.

decisions.what: multipleStatements enabled so the borrow flow could send three dependent statements in one round trip, four for reserve-then-borrow.
decisions.why: Batching, on a flow that touches three tables at once.
decisions.instead: A real transaction — which is what this actually needed, since batching buys throughput and explicitly not atomicity.

decisions.what: Book covers stored as longblob in MySQL and base64-encoded on every read.
decisions.why: It put everything in one place and one backup.
decisions.instead: Writing to disk with a path in the row — multer already writes the upload, and the code reads that file back purely to move its bytes into the database. The alternative was the better choice.

projects.title: Werewolf Game Moderator
projects.tagline: Android app that runs the moderator's role for an in-person game of Werewolf
projects.context: Final project, CS361 Mobile Application Development
projects.summary: The moderator's job in Werewolf is pure state management, which made it a natural fit for an explicit phase state machine. The problem that made it interesting was physical rather than logical: how do you show one player their secret role on a phone everyone else can see?

highlights.text: Designed the moderator game logic: role allocation and shuffle, the day/night phase state machine, timed voting with forced resolution, and win-condition evaluation.
Built the secret-role reveal on the accelerometer: the phone must be turned face-down and back up, with haptic confirmation, before a role is committed and the device passes to the next player.
Implemented Activity logic and XML layouts in Android Studio, including screen flow and a hand-written animated-GIF view.

engineering.architecture: Nine Activities wired as a linear state machine through Intent extras, with no ViewModel, repository or singleton. The entire game state is one Parcelable ArrayList<Player> serialised into every Intent, alongside a 'time' string of day, night or seer that selects which behaviour a single shared GameActivity runs over one layout. The only durable state in the app is one SharedPreferences boolean.

decisions.what: A single-device moderator rather than networked play.
decisions.why: It turns the secret-role problem from a networking problem into a physical one — which is where the interesting design work ended up.
decisions.instead: One device per player over the network, which removes the problem entirely and with it the reason this project is worth discussing.

decisions.what: The role reveal is gated on hardware: a two-state accelerometer latch, face-down with haptic confirmation then face-up, before the player is committed.
decisions.why: The phone physically cannot be showing a role while it is being passed, which a button press cannot guarantee.
decisions.instead: A hold-to-reveal button, which is simpler and also works on devices without an accelerometer.

decisions.what: Animated GIFs rendered by a hand-written view driving android.graphics.Movie — frame time against uptimeMillis modulo duration, matrix scale derived in onSizeChanged, self-scheduling via invalidate().
decisions.why: Worth writing once to understand how a self-invalidating custom view actually works.
decisions.instead: Glide, which is declared in build.gradle and never imported — I took the dependency and then wrote the thing myself.
